newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK's Working Title makes its name in Hollywood.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK's Working Title makes its name in Hollywood.

text.p: With Oscar-nominated hits like "Four Weddings and a Funeral" and "Fargo" under its belt, Britain's Working Title Films has managed to make a name for itself in Hollywood.
But founder Tim Bevan can recall when the London-based production company was all too easily forgotten by American movie makers.
"It used to be that once you left Hollywood, you were out of their minds," he said.

"Whereas now that we have a track record and we're seen to be spending significant sums of money, and we have a presence there, it's not out of sight, out of mind. We're a serious contender," he added during a joint interview with co-chief executive Eric Fellner.
That knock-out record is enough to make any Hollywood producer jealous and rank Working Title among Britain's top film production companies.
For three years in a row, the company, part of Dutch-based music and film giant PolyGram NV, has landed Oscar nominations for its movies, with "Dead Man Walking" rounding out the trio.
As a result, Working Title stands out as one of PolyGram's most prestigious weapons as the firm does battle with Hollywood's giants.
"We're a European company that's been able to co-exist with Hollywood and come out with films that have been successful not only in the U.S. domestic market but all over the world," Bevan said.

Working Title's reported development fund of $10 million and production budget of $150 million means that it can afford to make a slate of movies each year, including two to three films in the $20-30 million range.
Those figures represent a massive mark-up from the producers' first films.
FROM INDEPENDENCE TO POLYGRAM
Bevan, 39, and Fellner, 37, started out as friendly rivals, graduating from the world of music videos in the early 1980s to hit it big with their first features.
Both men exude a sharp-eyed youthfulness. Bevan describes himself as the more impulsive of the two, quick to make decisions, whereas Fellner says he may take days to decide on a project.
"It actually works quite well because Tim sometimes forces me to make decisions quickly, and I sometimes slow him down," Fellner said.
Bevan set up Working Title in 1985 with a partner to produce "My Beautiful Laundrette", while Fellner, separately, did the punk-rock love story "Sid and Nancy".
"We got lucky with our first movies, but then we both went on to produce a bunch of crap that no one saw. And that's totally soul-destroying," Bevan said.
"Where we both arrived when we decided to work together, we said, 'I'm not going to produce 10 more films that no one's going to see'," he added.
Fellner nodded grimly at the memory.

"No one goes to see them, and you don't make any money, and you've deferred your fees and you've put your house up as collateral. And you think that there has to be a way of making this work," he said.
The solution came in 1991, when Fellner joined Working Title and Bevan sold the company to PolyGram.
Their status as "independent" producers under PolyGram gave them creative autonomy as well as access to their new parent's financial backing and global distribution network.

"It's just too fraught being an independent producer," Bevan said. "There's no money in production. The only part of this industry where there really is money is in ultimately owning catalogue and in distribution."
Working Title still produces some low-budget films, but it has moved away from them over the past five years.
"What the movie business is based on is making bigger movies with movie stars in them which are your insurance policies," Bevan said.
This shift in focus was marked by Working Title's most expensive film to date, "French Kiss", a 1995 romantic comedy starring Meg Ryan and Kevin Kline.
Although the movie got a mediocre reception from critics and movie-goers, it still managed to make a return on its investment.

"The film did $100-110 million worldwide, a very nice piece of business. And we were fairly confident to spend $30-35 million on the budget because we knew that that worst-case scenario was what we got," Bevan said.
A KNACK FOR PICKING WINNERS
Bevan and Fellner attribute their success to long-term relationships with successful film makers like actor Tim Robbins and writer/directors Joel and Ethan Coen.

In the case of the Coens, the relationship that led to the backing of "The Hudsucker Proxy", a commercial disappointment, paid off this year with "Fargo", which won Oscars for best actress and best original screenplay.
Working Title is also producing the Coens' next film, "The Big Lebowski", a comedy starring Jeff Bridges and John Goodman that is set to be released at the end of the year.
Among other projects, the firm is planning a follow-up to "Four Weddings", currently codenamed the "Notting Hill Project" after the trendy west London neighbourhood of the same name.
The film, written by "Four Weddings" writer Richard Curtis, may involve Hugh Grant and some of the actors from "Four Weddings" in a different story line.

Other movies slated for release this year include "Bean", based on the "Mr. Bean" television series starring comedian Rowan Atkinson, as well as "The Borrowers", a $30 million family flick laden with special effects.

Working Title also plans to make a live-action version of the British cult TV series "The Thunderbirds" and a historical drama, "Elizabeth I", which will be directed by "Bandit Queen" maker Shekhar Kapur.
Will any of these win Oscar nods in 1998?
"Don't hold your breath," Bevan said, laughing.
